items.title: Hackers May Have Breached FBI Database Used by Police Nationwide
items.summary: FBI investigates an apparent breach of its NCIC criminal database, raising concerns over sensitive law enforcement data and security. The FBI is investigating a possible breach of a database that police use to check arrest warrants and access criminal records. According to the BBC , US media reported the incident, citing two people familiar with the matter. The FBI has not publicly commented on the reports and did not respond to the BBC’s request for comment. The database is the National Crime Information Center (NCIC). Federal and local law enforcement agencies use it to share information about arrest warrants and background checks. Police officers also access it during traffic stops and investigations. According to the FBI, as of 2023, the NCIC contained more than 18 million active records across 22 databases and provided services to over 100,000 law enforcement and criminal justice organisations. Reports say the intrusion was found in recent days, and nobody has said when it happened, how the attackers got in, who they are, or whether they took anything. It’s also unclear whether the incident disrupted police access to the system. Bureau officials learned of it on Thursday, according to CNN. President Donald Trump briefly commented on the incident during a Fox News interview on Saturday. He said he had just learned about the breach, called it bad news and said he did not like it. He also suggested that the investigation might reveal information that officials would not otherwise have discovered. “But maybe we’ll learn things that we would’ve never learned otherwise,” Trump said. On Sunday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told Fox News that the FBI was investigating who was behind the incident. However, he did not share further details about the intrusion. The incident comes during a difficult week for US technology and government services. Several outages affected banking, air traffic control and other sectors. Officials say these disruptions were not caused by cyberattacks, although they have attracted the attention of lawmakers. It’s also not the first time the FBI suffered a cyber attack, in September, the ShinyHunters crime group claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff, around 38,000 people. ShinyHunters provided a possible technical explanation for the alleged intrusion. The group claims the exploitation of an Oracle PeopleSoft zero-day, reportedly using it to gain remote code execution through infrastructure connected to the FBI’s recruitment services. Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini ( SecurityAffairs – hacking, NCIC)

Bureau officials learned of it on Thursday, according to CNN.

items.title: Scanning from Subnet 109.160.32.0/24, (Mon, Nov 23rd)
items.summary: This subnet is assigned to a web hosting and virtual private server (VPS) provider BANATSYNC SRL with AS198364, located in Timisoara, Romania. This graph shows the DShield sensor activity over the past 90 days for this subnet and it is still ongoing as of this writing. Using the ES|QL query listed below, starting the query from the 1 September 2026, 159 IPs from this block scanned at least once to multiple times my DShield sensors against mostly the SSH service and when found, attempted and sometimes successfully login the sensor. This analysis from this subnet started on the 5 September 2026 and capture regularly by 2 separate DShield sensors. A review of both the firewall and cowrie logs, all IPs involved attempted to login into the SSH service with almost all (152 out 159) of them succeeding to login into the sensors using with the standard usernames (root, ubuntu, admin, etc.) using a single command ( uname -s -v -n -r -m ) followed by a immediate disconnection. One sensor received 127 unique IPs while the other received 134 unique IPs. The firewall logs show some interesting characteristics with a time-to-live mostly between 45 to 52 with some exception that also include ranges between 232 to 243. In order to understand the discrepancies, I reviewed the packet capture from each sensor and found some packets where 69 IPs stared with a static IPID of 54321 and every one of them had a TTL that range between 232 to 243. All the inbound backets behaved the same way, SYN, SYN-ACK, RST targeting various ports including TCP/2323, TCP/22 and TCP/2222 where the actors/bots sometimes after multiple attemps, successfully login. Using the logs from the DShield SIEM and selecting only the traffic with the IPID 54321 and reviewing the Vega-Lite graph, it is easy to see the activity was consistent with the previously identified 69 IPs that each time each IP would come live, the first packet was always starting with high TTL ( 230+ ) and the remainder packets were all using normal TTL related to a moderl Linux system. In order to inspect why this would be happening, using packet capture by the sensors based on matching high TTL for one specific IP address (109.160.32.146) and what appeared was interesting. Using tshark to replay the initial packet for 13 Nov 2026 started with a TTL of 239 and when that traffic responded with a reset (0x0004), the TTL was now 50. Any traffic that followed the first SYN packets all had TTL of 50 (picture below). This is a sample of 4 IPs (DSL query below) out of the 69 that shows the first packet starting with a TTL 230+ followed by normal TTL after the activity continue. Reviewing the reports from VirusTotal of those 4 IPs [ 7 ][ 8 ][ 9 ][ 10 ] shows all the same characteristics with SSH brute-force if SSH is listening and running some commands before disconnecting. Shodan Open Ports This is a random list of IPs checked against Shodan that list the same open ports. The two sample lists show these IPs have SSH available as the only service while other have nothing open. If the SSH service is listening, it is using 2 different version of Ubuntu 24.04 LTS and 26.04 LTS. Shodan Information about SSH TCP/22 109.160.32.34 SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_10.2p1 Ubuntu-2ubuntu3.2 (Ubuntu 26.04 LTS) 109.160.32.141 SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.6p1 Ubuntu-3ubuntu13 (Ubuntu 24.04 LTS) 109.160.32.147 SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.6p1 Ubuntu-3ubuntu13 (Ubuntu 24.04 LTS) 109.160.32.150 SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.6p1 Ubuntu-3ubuntu13 (Ubuntu 24.04 LTS) 109.160.32.200 SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_10.2p1 Ubuntu-2ubuntu3.2 (Ubuntu 26.04 LTS) Shodan No Open Port for this IP sample 109.160.32.12 109.160.32.66 109.160.32.80 109.160.32.88 Kibana Traffic Analysis with DSL and ES|QL DSL Query IP Range { "range": { "related.ip": { "gte": "109.160.32.0", "lte": "109.160.32.255" } } } DSL Query for IP with a TTL Greater than 230 { "range": { "network.ttl": { "gte": "230" } } } DSL Query IP with Low & High TTL { "terms": { "related.ip": [ "109.160.32.88", "109.160.32.141", "109.160.32.147", "109.160.32.150" ] } } ES|QL Query FROM cowrie* | WHERE event.reference == "no match" | WHERE CIDR_MATCH(related.ip, "109.160.32.0/24") | STATS BY related.ip FROM cowrie* | WHERE event.reference == "no match" | WHERE CIDR_MATCH(related.ip, "109.160.32.0/24") | WHERE network.ttl >= 230 | STATS BY network.ttl TShark Output This is the command used to verify the activity between low and high TTL: tshark.exe -nnr tcp2323_54321_random.pcap -T fields -e frame.time -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e ip.ttl -e tcp.flags [1] https://scamalytics.com [2] https://arxiv.org/html/2307.08490v1 [3] https://github.com/zmap/zmap [4] https://github.com/zmap/zmap/blob/main/src/probe_modules/packet.c [5] https://isc.sans.edu/tools/honeypot/ [6] https://github.com/bruneaug/DShield-SIEM/tree/main [7] https://www.virustotal.com/gui/ip-address/109.160.32.88 [8] https://www.virustotal.com/gui/ip-address/109.160.32.141 [9] https://www.virustotal.com/gui/ip-address/109.160.32.147 [10] https://www.virustotal.com/gui/ip-address/109.160.32.150 ----------- Guy Bruneau IPSS Inc. items.summary_html:
This subnet is assigned to a web hosting and virtual private server (VPS) provider BANATSYNC SRL with AS198364, located in Timisoara, Romania. This graph shows the DShield sensor activity over the past 90 days for this subnet and it is still ongoing as of this writing.

Using the ES|QL query listed below, starting the query from the 1 September 2026, 159 IPs from this block scanned at least once to multiple times my DShield sensors against mostly the SSH service and when found, attempted and sometimes successfully login the sensor. This analysis from this subnet started on the 5 September 2026 and capture regularly by 2 separate DShield sensors. 

A review of both the firewall and cowrie logs, all IPs involved attempted to login into the SSH service with almost all (152 out 159) of them succeeding to login into the sensors using with the standard usernames (root, ubuntu, admin, etc.) using a single command (uname -s -v -n -r -m) followed by a immediate disconnection. One sensor received 127 unique IPs while the other received 134 unique IPs. 

The firewall logs show some interesting characteristics with a time-to-live mostly between 45 to 52 with some exception that also include ranges between 232 to 243. In order to understand the discrepancies, I reviewed the packet capture from each sensor and found some packets where 69 IPs stared with a static IPID of 54321 and every one of them had a TTL that range between 232 to 243. All the inbound backets behaved the same way, SYN, SYN-ACK, RST targeting various ports including TCP/2323, TCP/22 and TCP/2222 where the actors/bots sometimes after multiple attemps, successfully login.

Using the logs from the DShield SIEM and selecting only the traffic with the IPID 54321 and reviewing the Vega-Lite graph, it is easy to see the activity was consistent with the previously identified 69 IPs that each time each IP would come live, the first packet was always starting with high TTL (230+) and the remainder packets were all using normal TTL related to a moderl Linux system. In order to inspect why this would be happening, using packet capture by the sensors based on matching high TTL for one specific IP address (109.160.32.146) and what appeared was interesting. Using tshark to replay the initial packet for 13 Nov 2026 started with a TTL of 239 and when that traffic responded with a reset (0x0004), the TTL was now 50. Any traffic that followed the first SYN packets all had TTL of 50 (picture below). 

This is a sample of 4 IPs (DSL query below) out of the 69 that shows the first packet starting with a TTL 230+ followed by normal TTL after the activity continue. Reviewing  the reports from VirusTotal of those 4 IPs [7][8][9][10] shows all the same characteristics with SSH brute-force if SSH is listening and running some commands before disconnecting.

Shodan Open Ports
This is a random list of IPs checked against Shodan that list the same open ports. The two sample lists show these IPs have SSH available as the only service while other have nothing open. If the SSH service is listening, it is using 2 different version of Ubuntu 24.04 LTS and 26.04 LTS.

items.title: LinkedIn Will Drop Your Connections’ Emails, Employers and Job Titles From Its Data Download
items.summary: LinkedIn is about to strip the most useful columns from the list of connections you can download about yourself. A short notice under the Request archive button on LinkedIn’s data download page, which we checked on our own account, says that as of December 2026 the download “no longer includes your connections’ email addresses, current companies, or job titles.” It adds that you can still see whatever your connections share on their profiles, including contact details they make available to you. It gives no date and no reason. Names, profile links and the date you connected stay. LinkedIn hasn’t announced the change anywhere else we could find. Recruiter Jan Tegze, who wrote about it on Sunday, found no blog post or press release, and LinkedIn’s own help page on downloading your data still described the old file when we read it early on Tuesday. The notice was circulating on LinkedIn and X by 20 November and reached Hacker News on Monday. We found no coverage by larger outlets as we published. We’ve asked LinkedIn for comment.
items.summary_html:
LinkedIn is about to strip the most useful columns from the list of connections you can download about yourself.

A short notice under the Request archive button on LinkedIn’s data download page, which we checked on our own account, says that as of December 2026 the download “no longer includes your connections’ email addresses, current companies, or job titles.” It adds that you can still see whatever your connections share on their profiles, including contact details they make available to you. It gives no date and no reason. Names, profile links and the date you connected stay.

LinkedIn hasn’t announced the change anywhere else we could find. Recruiter Jan Tegze, who wrote about it on Sunday, found no blog post or press release, and LinkedIn’s own help page on downloading your data still described the old file when we read it early on Tuesday. The notice was circulating on LinkedIn and X by 20 November and reached Hacker News on Monday. We found no coverage by larger outlets as we published. We’ve asked LinkedIn for comment.

items.title: Ethereum Foundation doubles protocol security team ahead of overhaul
items.summary: The foundation said its next upgrade will be harder than the Merge, and the required pace of development will make it easier to ship bugs.

items.title: Hackers breach Austrian Foreign Ministry website, access diplomats' contact details
items.summary: Austria's Foreign Ministry said late last week that hackers breached one of its websites and accessed the names and official contact information of employees at its Vienna headquarters and at Austria’s diplomatic missions abroad.

items.summary: Spain’s professional soccer league LaLiga said Monday hackers stole personal information belonging to fans in a cyberattack affecting its digital services and those of several Spanish clubs.

items.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ hacker sentenced to seven years, released the same day
items.summary: A British cybercriminal who hacked Rockstar Games and leaked footage of Grand Theft Auto VI was sentenced Monday to seven years in prison, and then released on license because of time served.
